newsitem.title: USA: Mississippi is first to settle tobacco suit.
newsitem.headline: Mississippi is first to settle tobacco suit.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

Mississippi's top legal officer Thursday announced a last-minute $3.36 billion settlement of the state's Medicaid lawsuit against the tobacco industry, averting the first trial of 40 such cases across the country.

While Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore said payments to the state continue "forever" under the pact, he urged Congress and the White House to approve last month's historic $368.5 billion national accord that would take precedence over the state agreement.
"I'm pleading for the president and the Congress to pass this bill," Moore told reporters at a Jackson, Miss., news conference.
"All the things that will help our children will have to be passed by the national Congress. We've provided the leverage so that Congress can now act," he said.
The nation's four largest tobacco companies also issued a joint statement urging the passage of national legislation.

"The settlement resolves certain legal and financial issues in one state, but it does not -- and could not -- address broader issues of concern in Mississippi and throughout the nation," the companies said.
"Today's state action ends one case, but it does not end the need for a national solution of the tobacco conflict," they said.
Under the agreement, the companies would pay Mississippi more than $3.36 billion over a 25-year period. The first payment of $170 million is due by July 15.
Beginning in December 1998, they will pay Mississippi a 1.7 percent share of the part of the annual payments that are contemplated to be paid to the states in the large settlement.
Without adjusting for inflation and changes in sales volume, this could result in payments to Mississippi of $68 million in 1998 and $76.5 million in 1999.
The payments to Mississippi will scale up to $136 million by the sixth year and continue at that level.

"I think it (Mississippi settlement) is dramatic evidence that Big Tobacco wants to avoid trials because it knows it will lose and wants to escape mountains of evidence showing decades of wrongdoing that would be exposed in a public trial," Connecticut Attorney General Richard Blumenthal said.
However, he also pointed out that the agreement did not mean that the remaining 39 states that have sued the tobacco industry would be able to reach settlements.
Florida Attorney General Bob Butterworth, whose case is scheduled for trial on Aug. 4, said Thursday that no deal was imminent to settle the state's $1 billion Medicaid lawsuit.
He said he last met tobacco negotiators on June 26 and did not expect to bargain again for at least another two weeks.

"We're four weeks away from jury selection. It'll be another month before a judge will hear opening statements .... Given the fact our case is at least a couple months away, I think it would be a little premature for both sides to discuss settlement in the Florida case," he said.

In Texas, where the state's Medicaid trial is scheduled to begin Sept. 29, a spokeswoman for the attorney general's office said no negotiations are being held now with the tobacco industry. She said the state is preparing for trial.
Minnesota Attorney General Hubert Humphrey, who has opposed the terms of the national settlement, vowed to keep fighting his lawsuit.

"The Mississippi settlement is an acknowledgment that aggressive pursuit of the states' lawsuits is the best path to justice," he said. "The over-$3 billion settlement sets a minimum floor for those states with antitrust, consumer fraud, and treble damages claims that were not even alleged in the Mississippi case."
Mississippi was the first state to sue the industry, in May 1994, seeking to recoup $940 million in Medicaid costs of treating sick smokers.
Moore had given the industry a Thursday afternoon deadline to reach a settlement or proceed with what would have been a historic trial.
